prompt: What is the difference between cost per API call and cost per completed task, and why does it change decisions?
answer_markdown: Cost per call is just the token bill for one request. Cost per completed task includes everything needed to actually finish the job: retries when the output fails validation, the second attempt when the first answer is wrong, and the human who handles it when the model gives up. It changes decisions because the two can point in opposite directions. A small model at a fraction of the price per call but a 28% failure rate pushes roughly a tenth of tasks to a human at several dollars each, which can make it far more expensive per completed task than a model costing twenty times more per call. Any 'we switched to a cheaper model to save money' story that never measured completion rate is likely to have increased total cost while improving the metric being watched. Measure the failure rate and the downstream cost of failure before comparing models at all.

prompt: Does streaming make an LLM response faster? Explain what it actually changes.
answer_markdown: No — total generation time is essentially unchanged, because the model still produces the same number of tokens at the same rate. What streaming changes is when the user sees the first one. Without streaming they wait for the entire response, which for a long answer might be several seconds of apparent nothing; with streaming, text starts appearing after the time-to-first-token, typically a few hundred milliseconds, and then flows continuously. Perceived responsiveness is dominated by that first-token latency rather than total duration, so streaming transforms the experience without touching the underlying speed. It is worth doing by default on anything user-facing because the effort is small and the perceptual difference is large. Two caveats worth mentioning: streaming complicates output validation, since you cannot validate a schema until the response is complete, and it complicates guardrails that need to inspect the full output before showing anything — which is why some safety-critical flows deliberately do not stream.

prompt: You enabled prompt caching but your cache hit rate is near zero. What is the most likely cause?
answer_markdown: Something variable is sitting at the front of your prompt. Prefix caching works by matching an exact byte-identical prefix, so the cache only helps for the portion of the prompt before the first difference. If your system prompt begins with a timestamp, a request ID, a session ID, a user name, or the current date, every request has a unique prefix from the very first tokens and nothing is ever reused. The fix is to restructure the prompt so all static content comes first — the system prompt, tool definitions, few-shot examples — and everything variable goes last: retrieved context, conversation history, and the user's message. Also check that the cached section is long enough to qualify, since providers set a minimum prefix length below which caching does not activate, and that you are not changing tool definitions or system prompt wording between requests in ways you did not intend. Verify by reading the cached-token count in the API's usage response rather than assuming, since that number tells you directly how much of the prefix was reused.

prompt: When would you use a batch API, and when is it the wrong choice?
answer_markdown: Use it when no user is waiting and the work is known in advance: nightly classification of a support-ticket backlog, generating embeddings for an entire corpus during an initial index build, backfilling summaries over historical data, or running a large evaluation suite. Batch APIs typically offer around half the cost with a turnaround measured in hours and access to a separate, much higher rate limit pool, which is what makes large backfills feasible at all. It is the wrong choice for anything interactive — a chat reply, a search query, an agent step — because the latency is orders of magnitude beyond what a waiting user tolerates, and no discount compensates for a feature that appears broken. The design implication is that these are architecturally different paths rather than a flag you flip: batch work needs job tracking, result reconciliation, and partial-failure handling, since a batch containing tens of thousands of requests will have some that fail and need retrying independently.

prompt: Explain how you would decide whether a model cascade is worth building.
answer_markdown: Compute the expected cost per completed task including the escalation path, rather than comparing per-call prices. A cascade tries a cheap model first, checks whether the result is good enough, and escalates to an expensive model when it is not — which means you pay the cheap model's cost on every single request plus the expensive model's cost on every escalation, plus the cost of whatever quality check decides between them. That only wins when the cheap model succeeds often enough that escalations stay rare; at a low success rate you are paying for both models on most requests and would have been better off using the strong model alone. The quality check itself needs scrutiny too: if it is another LLM call it adds real cost and latency, whereas a deterministic check like schema validation or a confidence threshold is nearly free and is what makes cascades economical. Also weigh the latency cost, since an escalated request pays both models' generation time sequentially. Run the numbers with your own measured success rates and be prepared for the answer to be that a cascade is not worth the added complexity.

prompt: Your team needs to halve LLM spend without degrading quality. Walk through your approach.
answer_markdown: Measure before changing anything: log prompt tokens, completion tokens, and cost per request, then find where spend actually concentrates — it is usually a small number of endpoints or a long tail of unusually large requests rather than uniform usage. Then work through the changes from lowest to highest risk. Restructure prompts so static content sits at the front and enable prefix caching, which often gives a large reduction with zero quality impact. Cap output length with max_tokens and an instruction to be concise, since completion tokens are priced higher than prompt tokens and also dominate latency. Trim what you are sending: unnecessary few-shot examples, over-long system prompts, and too many retrieved chunks all cost on every call. Add caching for repeated queries, starting with exact-match and adding semantic caching only with a conservative threshold, since a loose one serves wrong answers. Only then consider routing simple requests to a smaller model, and validate that specifically against your eval set because it is the change most likely to cost more in the end through increased failures. Gate every change on the golden dataset so a quality regression surfaces before users find it.
